title: Moving Coil Galvanometer
notes: A moving-coil galvanometer has a coil of N turns and area A in the radial magnetic field of a cylindrical pole piece. The field is radial so that the plane of the coil stays parallel to B in the useful sense and the torque is N I A B for any deflection.
A hairspring provides a restoring torque k θ. At equilibrium N I A B = k θ, so θ is proportional to I. The scale can be linear.

Current sensitivity is the deflection per unit current, N A B / k. Voltage sensitivity is the deflection per unit voltage. A large N, a large area, a strong field or a weak spring increases sensitivity.

To make an ammeter, a small shunt resistor is connected in parallel so that most of the current bypasses the coil. The galvanometer then reads a large current with only a small current through the coil.
To make a voltmeter, a large resistor is connected in series so that the instrument draws little current and can be placed across a component.
The coil is wound on a conducting frame, or has a separate damper, so that eddy currents stop the oscillation and the needle settles.
confusion: ❌ 'A galvanometer measures current directly like an ammeter.' ✅ A galvanometer detects *small* currents; an ammeter is a galvanometer with a *shunt resistor* added in parallel to measure larger currents.
❌ 'Increasing the number of turns reduces sensitivity.' ✅ Sensitivity is *directly proportional* to the number of turns (N): more turns = greater deflection for the same current.
❌ 'A galvanometer has zero resistance.' ✅ It has a *finite* resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance, but the galvanometer itself does not.
The shunt is parallel, not series.
The voltmeter multiplier is series, not parallel.
Sensitivity is not the same as the range.
The radial field is what keeps the torque independent of angle.
